claim: Helical polymers are found throughout biology and account for a substantial fraction of the protein in a cell.
source: Helical polymers are found throughout biology and account for a substantial fraction of the protein in a cell.
evidence: This is a general statement about the prevalence of helical polymers in biological systems, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Projections of helical filaments show many different views of identical subunits in identical environments.
source: These filaments are very attractive for three-dimensional reconstruction from electron micrographs due to the fact that projections of these filaments show many different views of identical subunits in identical environments.
evidence: This describes a fundamental property of helical symmetry that is well-established in structural biology.

claim: Ambiguities exist in defining the symmetry of a helical filament when one has limited resolution.
source: However, ambiguities exist in defining the symmetry of a helical filament when one has limited resolution, and mistakes can be made.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published examples and the author's expertise in the field.

claim: Until one reaches a near-atomic level of resolution, there are not necessarily reality-checks that can distinguish between correct and incorrect solutions.
source: Until one reaches a near-atomic level of resolution, there are not necessarily reality-checks that can distinguish between correct and incorrect solutions.
evidence: This is based on the author's experience and understanding of helical reconstruction methodology.

claim: Xu et al. (2014) almost certainly imposed an incorrect helical symmetry.
source: A recent paper in eLife (Xu et al., 2014) almost certainly imposed an incorrect helical symmetry and this can be seen using filament images posted by Xu et al.
evidence: This claim is supported by the author's reanalysis of the deposited data from Xu et al., presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Helical polymers are ubiquitous in biology and are found extensively in viruses.
source: Helical polymers are ubiquitous in biology, and are found extensively in viruses (Ge and Zhou, 2011), bacteria (Polka et al., 2009; Ozyamak et al., 2013), eukaryotes (Galkin et al., 2010) and archaea (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Helical polymers are found extensively in bacteria.
source: Helical polymers are ubiquitous in biology, and are found extensively in viruses (Ge and Zhou, 2011), bacteria (Polka et al., 2009; Ozyamak et al., 2013), eukaryotes (Galkin et al., 2010) and archaea (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Helical polymers are found extensively in eukaryotes.
source: Helical polymers are ubiquitous in biology, and are found extensively in viruses (Ge and Zhou, 2011), bacteria (Polka et al., 2009; Ozyamak et al., 2013), eukaryotes (Galkin et al., 2010) and archaea (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Helical polymers are found extensively in archaea.
source: Helical polymers are ubiquitous in biology, and are found extensively in viruses (Ge and Zhou, 2011), bacteria (Polka et al., 2009; Ozyamak et al., 2013), eukaryotes (Galkin et al., 2010) and archaea (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Identical subunits in helical filaments are rotated and translated along a filament axis.
source: Because of the symmetry inherent in helical filaments (where identical subunits are rotated and translated along a filament axis) projections of helical filaments can provide all of the information needed to generate a three-dimensional reconstruction from a limited number of images
evidence: This describes the fundamental mathematical property of helical symmetry.

claim: The first electron microscopic three dimensional reconstruction was made from a helical bacteriophage tail.
source: this property was exploited in the first electron microscopic (EM) three dimensional reconstruction, which was made from a helical bacteriophage tail (DeRosier and Klug, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the seminal work by DeRosier and Klug.

claim: New advances in computational approaches have meant that the determination of structures of helical polymers at near-atomic resolution is becoming much more common.
source: New advances in both computational approaches (Egelman, 2000) and cryo-imaging with direct electron detectors (Bai et al., 2013) have meant that the determination of structures of helical polymers at near-atomic resolution (Lu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014) is becoming much more common.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological advances and high-resolution structures.

claim: New advances in cryo-imaging with direct electron detectors have meant that the determination of structures of helical polymers at near-atomic resolution is becoming much more common.
source: New advances in both computational approaches (Egelman, 2000) and cryo-imaging with direct electron detectors (Bai et al., 2013) have meant that the determination of structures of helical polymers at near-atomic resolution (Lu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014) is becoming much more common.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent technological advances and high-resolution structures.

claim: The assignment of the correct symmetry to a helical polymer can still be problematic.
source: However, the assignment of the correct symmetry to a helical polymer can still be problematic (Egelman, 2010; Desfosses et al., 2014), and examples exist where the wrong symmetry has been mistakenly imposed (Okorokov et al., 2010; Sen et al., 2010; Yu and Egelman, 2010; Heymann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature discussing these challenges.

claim: Examples exist where the wrong symmetry has been mistakenly imposed in helical reconstruction.
source: However, the assignment of the correct symmetry to a helical polymer can still be problematic (Egelman, 2010; Desfosses et al., 2014), and examples exist where the wrong symmetry has been mistakenly imposed (Okorokov et al., 2010; Sen et al., 2010; Yu and Egelman, 2010; Heymann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to specific cases where incorrect symmetry was imposed.

claim: Solutions may be obtained that are stable under iterative refinement, consistent with the images, but simply wrong.
source: Insufficient understanding exists about how solutions (three-dimensional structures) may be obtained that are stable under iterative refinement, consistent with the images, but simply wrong.
evidence: This is based on the author's experience and observations in the field of helical reconstruction.

claim: Wrong solutions arise from imposing a helical symmetry that is incorrect when the available resolution does not allow one to distinguish between wrong symmetries and the correct one.
source: This arises from imposing a helical symmetry that is incorrect, but the available resolution does not allow one to distinguish between wrong symmetries and the correct one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the author's analysis and understanding of helical reconstruction methodology.

claim: The reconstruction of the MAVS filament by Wu et al. had a stated resolution of 3.6 Å.
source: The reconstruction of the MAVS filament presented in Wu et al. had a stated resolution of 3.6 Å and had a helical symmetry of a rotation of −101.1° (the negative rotation corresponding to a left-handed helix) and a rise of 5.1 Å per subunit.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the published results from Wu et al.

claim: The reconstruction of the MAVS filament by Wu et al. had a helical symmetry of a rotation of −101.1° and a rise of 5.1 Å per subunit.
source: The reconstruction of the MAVS filament presented in Wu et al. had a stated resolution of 3.6 Å and had a helical symmetry of a rotation of −101.1° (the negative rotation corresponding to a left-handed helix) and a rise of 5.1 Å per subunit.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the published results from Wu et al.

claim: A negative rotation corresponds to a left-handed helix.
source: The reconstruction of the MAVS filament presented in Wu et al. had a stated resolution of 3.6 Å and had a helical symmetry of a rotation of −101.1° (the negative rotation corresponding to a left-handed helix) and a rise of 5.1 Å per subunit.
evidence: This is a standard convention in helical reconstruction.

claim: The reconstruction of the MAVS filament by Xu et al. had a stated resolution of 9.6 Å.
source: In contrast, the reconstruction of Xu et al. had a stated resolution of 9.6 Å, a C3 point group rotational symmetry, with a rotation of −53.6° and a rise of 16.8 Å for every ring of three subunits.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the published results from Xu et al.

claim: The reconstruction of the MAVS filament by Xu et al. had a C3 point group rotational symmetry, with a rotation of −53.6° and a rise of 16.8 Å for every ring of three subunits.
source: In contrast, the reconstruction of Xu et al. had a stated resolution of 9.6 Å, a C3 point group rotational symmetry, with a rotation of −53.6° and a rise of 16.8 Å for every ring of three subunits.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the published results from Xu et al.

claim: In the Wu et al. reconstruction, α-helices are clearly resolved.
source: One of the differences between the two reconstructions is that in Wu et al. not only are α-helices clearly resolved, but bulky aromatic side-chains can be seen that are consistent with not only the sequence but a crystal structure of the subunit which can be fit quite well as a rigid body into the reconstruction.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the features visible in the Wu et al. reconstruction.

claim: In the Wu et al. reconstruction, bulky aromatic side-chains can be seen that are consistent with the sequence.
source: One of the differences between the two reconstructions is that in Wu et al. not only are α-helices clearly resolved, but bulky aromatic side-chains can be seen that are consistent with not only the sequence but a crystal structure of the subunit which can be fit quite well as a rigid body into the reconstruction.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the features visible in the Wu et al. reconstruction and their consistency with known data.

claim: A crystal structure of the MAVS subunit can be fit quite well as a rigid body into the Wu et al. reconstruction.
source: One of the differences between the two reconstructions is that in Wu et al. not only are α-helices clearly resolved, but bulky aromatic side-chains can be seen that are consistent with not only the sequence but a crystal structure of the subunit which can be fit quite well as a rigid body into the reconstruction.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the compatibility of the Wu et al. reconstruction with crystallographic data.

claim: Xu et al. do not dispute the validity of the reconstruction in Wu et al.
source: In the Comment appended to their paper (Jiang, 2014), Xu et al. do not dispute the validity of the reconstruction in Wu et al., but argue that the filament being reconstructed by Wu et al. is an artifact of harsh preparative procedures, and that their filaments have a different symmetry and represent a more native conformation.
evidence: This is a statement about the position taken by Xu et al. in their published comment.

claim: Xu et al. argue that the filament being reconstructed by Wu et al. is an artifact of harsh preparative procedures.
source: In the Comment appended to their paper (Jiang, 2014), Xu et al. do not dispute the validity of the reconstruction in Wu et al., but argue that the filament being reconstructed by Wu et al. is an artifact of harsh preparative procedures, and that their filaments have a different symmetry and represent a more native conformation.
evidence: This is a statement about the argument made by Xu et al. in their published comment.

claim: Xu et al. argue that their filaments have a different symmetry and represent a more native conformation.
source: In the Comment appended to their paper (Jiang, 2014), Xu et al. do not dispute the validity of the reconstruction in Wu et al., but argue that the filament being reconstructed by Wu et al. is an artifact of harsh preparative procedures, and that their filaments have a different symmetry and represent a more native conformation.
evidence: This is a statement about the argument made by Xu et al. in their published comment.

claim: The authors of Xu et al. have deposited the images that they used in the EMPIAR database.
source: Given that the authors of Xu et al. have deposited the images that they used in the EMPIAR database, these arguments can be directly tested.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data availability that can be verified.

claim: The power spectrum of an image is the central section of the three-dimensional power spectrum of the object being projected onto the image.
source: Figure 1 shows how the power spectrum of an image is the central section of the three-dimensional power spectrum of the object being projected onto the image.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of Fourier analysis applied to projection imaging, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The projection is sensitive to any tilt of the axis of the object out of the plane of projection.
source: As such, the projection is sensitive to any tilt of the axis of the object out of the plane of projection.
evidence: This is a consequence of the projection theorem in Fourier analysis.

claim: An untilted central section would generate two separated peaks on both sides of the meridian.
source: An untilted central section (Figure 1B) would generate the two separated peaks on both sides of the meridian seen in Figure 1D (arrow), while a sufficiently tilted central section (Figure 1C) would generate a single intensity on the meridian (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1 and is based on the principles of Fourier analysis.

claim: A sufficiently tilted central section would generate a single intensity on the meridian.
source: An untilted central section (Figure 1B) would generate the two separated peaks on both sides of the meridian seen in Figure 1D (arrow), while a sufficiently tilted central section (Figure 1C) would generate a single intensity on the meridian (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1 and is based on the principles of Fourier analysis.

claim: For negatively stained polymers, where filaments are adsorbed to a carbon film, out-of-plane tilt can be largely ignored.
source: For negatively stained polymers, where filaments are adsorbed to a carbon film, out-of-plane tilt can be largely ignored.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the behavior of negatively stained specimens.

claim: In cryo-EM, where filaments are imaged within an ice film of finite thickness, out-of-plane tilt cannot be ignored.
source: In cryo-EM, where filaments are imaged within an ice film of finite thickness, such tilt cannot be ignored, particularly as one becomes more sensitive to it the higher the resolution.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cryo-EM imaging conditions.

claim: One becomes more sensitive to out-of-plane tilt the higher the resolution.
source: In cryo-EM, where filaments are imaged within an ice film of finite thickness, such tilt cannot be ignored, particularly as one becomes more sensitive to it the higher the resolution.
evidence: This is based on the principles of high-resolution imaging and Fourier analysis.

claim: There was substantial out-of-plane tilt for the filaments imaged by Xu et al.
source: The large peaks at −20° and +20° correspond to segments with tilt angles greater than 20°, showing the unexpectedly large degree of tilt for these filaments.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the histogram in Figure 2A generated from the author's analysis of the Xu et al. data.

claim: When only taking segments with tilt angles in the three central bins (−4°, 0°, +4°), a power spectrum is generated that clearly shows an n = −1 layer line with no intensity on the meridian.
source: If one only takes the segments in the three central bins (−4°, 0°, +4°) a power spectrum is generated (Figure 2B) that clearly shows (arrow) an n = −1 layer line with no intensity on the meridian.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the power spectrum shown in Figure 2B from the author's analysis.

claim: The power spectrum from untilted segments of Xu et al. filaments looks the same as that shown by Wu et al.
source: This power spectrum looks to be the same as that shown by Wu et al., undercutting the argument that the filaments being used by the two groups are different.
evidence: This is based on visual comparison of power spectra from the author's analysis.

claim: The tilt needed to make the two separated peaks appear as a single peak on the meridian is approximately 9°.
source: One can calculate the tilt that would be needed to make the two separated peaks in Figure 2B appear as a single peak on the meridian, and it is ∼9°, entirely consistent with the histogram in Figure 2A.
evidence: This is based on a calculation performed by the author using the data.

claim: A stable solution in IHRSR is a necessary, but not sufficient, requirement for the solution to be correct.
source: I have argued (Egelman, 2007, 2010) that a stable solution in IHRSR is a necessary, but not sufficient, requirement for the solution to be correct, since it has been clear that many wrong solutions can also be stable.
evidence: This is based on the author's previous publications and experience with the IHRSR method.

claim: Many wrong solutions can be stable in IHRSR.
source: I have argued (Egelman, 2007, 2010) that a stable solution in IHRSR is a necessary, but not sufficient, requirement for the solution to be correct, since it has been clear that many wrong solutions can also be stable.
evidence: This is based on the author's previous publications and experience with the IHRSR method.

claim: In cryo-EM, when out-of-plane tilt cannot be ignored, correct solutions can be unstable when this tilt is ignored.
source: However, it has become apparent in cryo-EM, when out-of-plane tilt cannot be ignored, that correct solutions can be unstable when this tilt is ignored.
evidence: This is based on the author's experience and observations in cryo-EM helical reconstruction.

claim: The symmetry determined by Wu et al. can be applied to the filaments of Xu et al. and is stable in IHRSR cycles.
source: It can be seen that the symmetry determined by Wu et al. can be applied to the filaments of Xu et al. and that this is quite stable in IHRSR cycles, again undercutting their argument that the two sets of filaments are different.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 3 showing the stability of symmetry parameters over IHRSR cycles.

claim: Xu et al. correctly state that a hole can be seen in their filaments independently of the symmetry simply by cylindrically averaging their 3D density map.
source: They correctly state that such a hole can be seen in their filaments independently of the symmetry simply by cylindrically averaging their 3D density map.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a correct observation by Xu et al.

claim: When the cryo-EM density map deposited by Wu et al. (EMDB-5922) is filtered to 12 Å resolution, a hole is seen in the center.
source: If one takes the cryo-EM density map deposited by Wu et al. (EMDB-5922) and filters it to 12 Å resolution a hole is seen in the center (Figure 4B, arrow).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the author's analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The subunits in the Wu et al. model are helically arranged and do not pack to form a solid core.
source: The reason that this is consistent with the deposited model (3j6j.PDB) is simply that the subunits are helically arranged and do not pack to form a solid core.
evidence: This is based on examination of the deposited atomic model.

claim: The packing of protein is less dense in the center of the filament than it is at higher radius.
source: Since the packing of protein is less dense in the center of the filament than it is at higher radius, a cylindrically averaged density distribution will show a continuous hole in the center of the filament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the helical arrangement of subunits in the model.

claim: A cylindrically averaged density distribution will show a continuous hole in the center of the filament when protein packing is less dense in the center.
source: Since the packing of protein is less dense in the center of the filament than it is at higher radius, a cylindrically averaged density distribution will show a continuous hole in the center of the filament.
evidence: This is based on the principles of density averaging and the geometry of helical structures.

claim: The actual resolution of the reconstruction generated from the images of Xu et al. is 12 Å.
source: The reason that I have chosen 12 Å for this comparison is that this is the actual resolution of the reconstruction (Figure 4A,C) that I have been able to generate from the images of Xu et al.
evidence: This is based on the author's reanalysis of the Xu et al. data.

claim: The Xu et al. images appear to be from thick ice.
source: Why is the resolution so poor? The most obvious differences are that the Xu et al. images appear to be from thick ice, there is a very noisy background, and they have applied a carbon film which degrades the signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is based on the author's examination of the deposited images.

claim: The Xu et al. images have a very noisy background.
source: Why is the resolution so poor? The most obvious differences are that the Xu et al. images appear to be from thick ice, there is a very noisy background, and they have applied a carbon film which degrades the signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is based on the author's examination of the deposited images.

claim: Xu et al. have applied a carbon film which degrades the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Why is the resolution so poor? The most obvious differences are that the Xu et al. images appear to be from thick ice, there is a very noisy background, and they have applied a carbon film which degrades the signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is based on the author's examination of the deposited images and knowledge of how carbon films affect image quality.

claim: Since Xu et al. are sampling at 2.3 Å/px, the best one might hope to achieve would be approximately 7 Å resolution (2/3 Nyquist).
source: Since they are sampling at 2.3 Å/px, the best one might hope to achieve would be ∼7 Å resolution (2/3 Nyquist) but given the problems with the images one would never get even close to this.
evidence: This is based on the Nyquist sampling theorem and standard expectations in cryo-EM.

claim: The three arguments for why their filaments are different from those of Wu et al., advanced by Xu et al. in their Comment, are not true.
source: I have thus shown that the three arguments for why their filaments are different from those of Wu et al., advanced by Xu et al. in their Comment, are not true.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the author's reanalysis of the Xu et al. data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Establishing that the filaments are the same would require a high resolution reconstruction from the filaments of Xu et al. which would be impossible.
source: This does not establish, however, that the filaments are the same. Establishing that would require a high resolution reconstruction from the filaments of Xu et al. which I fear would be impossible.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the poor quality of the Xu et al. images.

claim: The great success of protein x-ray crystallography lies in the fact that structures are being solved that all have a known stereochemistry.
source: The great success of protein x-ray crystallography lies in the fact that structures are being solved that all have a known stereochemistry.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about protein crystallography.

claim: At lower resolution by EM most reality-checks are simply absent.
source: At lower resolution by EM most of these reality-checks are simply absent, and one needs to generate methods, such as the tilt-pair validation used for single-particle cryo-EM (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003) that can distinguish between correct and incorrect reconstructions.
evidence: This is based on the author's knowledge and experience in the field of cryo-EM.

claim: Tilt-pair validation is used for single-particle cryo-EM to distinguish between correct and incorrect reconstructions.
source: At lower resolution by EM most of these reality-checks are simply absent, and one needs to generate methods, such as the tilt-pair validation used for single-particle cryo-EM (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003) that can distinguish between correct and incorrect reconstructions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the published method.

claim: As the field of cryo-EM is now rapidly moving to near-atomic resolution, seeing recognizable secondary structure provides a necessary and sufficient validation of a reconstruction.
source: As the field of cryo-EM is now rapidly moving to near-atomic resolution, seeing recognizable secondary structure provides a necessary and sufficient validation of a reconstruction.
evidence: This is based on the author's knowledge and the current state of the cryo-EM field.

claim: In the case of Wu et al., having a map with near-atomic detail showing right-handed α-helices confirmed not only the symmetry but the absolute hand of the reconstruction.
source: In the case of Wu et al. having a map with near-atomic detail, showing right-handed α-helices, confirmed not only the symmetry but the absolute hand of the reconstruction, whereas in the absence of this level of detail one must use means such as metal-shadowing or tomography to resolve the enantiomorphic ambiguity present.
evidence: This is based on the properties of the Wu et al. reconstruction and the principles of structural validation.

claim: In the absence of near-atomic detail, one must use means such as metal-shadowing or tomography to resolve the enantiomorphic ambiguity.
source: In the case of Wu et al. having a map with near-atomic detail, showing right-handed α-helices, confirmed not only the symmetry but the absolute hand of the reconstruction, whereas in the absence of this level of detail one must use means such as metal-shadowing or tomography to resolve the enantiomorphic ambiguity present.
evidence: This is based on established methods in the field for determining handedness.

claim: There is vanishingly little agreement between the deposited map (EMDB-5890) and the deposited model (PDB 3j6c) of Xu et al.
source: Unfortunately, there is vanishingly little agreement between their deposited map (EMDB-5890) and their deposited model (PDB 3j6c).
evidence: This is based on the author's comparison of the deposited data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: At higher thresholds, there is no match between the features in the Xu et al. reconstruction and their model.
source: One sees at these higher thresholds than used in Xu et al. that there is actually no match between the features in one and in the other.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 5.

claim: A 9 Å resolution reconstruction of an actin-cofilin filament shows an excellent match with an atomic model filtered to this resolution.
source: In a 9 Å resolution reconstruction of an actin-cofilin filament a comparison with an atomic model filtered to this resolution (Supplementary figure 1D, Galkin et al., 2011) shows an excellent match.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published example.

claim: A 7.5 Å resolution reconstruction of a naked actin filament shows an excellent match with an atomic model filtered to this resolution.
source: Similarly, a 7.5 Å resolution reconstruction of a naked actin filament shows an excellent match with an atomic model filtered to this resolution (Supplementary figure 2, Fujii et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published example.

claim: A Fourier Shell Correlation between the Xu et al. model and reconstruction shows that at FSC = 0.5 the resolution is approximately 22 Å.
source: A Fourier Shell Correlation between their model and reconstruction (E) shows that at FSC = 0.5 the resolution is ∼22 Å, which is consistent with the visual comparison of the map and model (A–D).
evidence: This is based on the author's quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A resolution of approximately 22 Å suggests that the only agreement between the map and the model is for compact 'blobs' related by the same imposed helical symmetry.
source: Such a resolution suggests that the only agreement between the map and the model is for compact 'blobs' (which is what this small subunit looks like at a resolution of 22 Å) related by the same imposed helical symmetry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FSC analysis and understanding of what features are visible at different resolutions.

claim: The comparison between the map and model should have raised questions about whether the helical symmetry imposed was actually correct.
source: This type of comparison, had it been done by the authors, should have raised many questions. One is whether the helical symmetry imposed was actually correct.
evidence: This is a critical inference based on the poor agreement between map and model.

claim: The FSC may not have any meaning in the Xu et al. case since it yields such a different result between two reconstructions and between the overall reconstruction and the model.
source: Another is whether the FSC, which is only a measure of internal consistency between two halves of the image set and not a measure of actual resolution, has any meaning in this instance since it yields such a different result between two reconstructions (each generated from half of the image set) and between the overall reconstruction and the model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between different resolution estimates.

claim: The arguments of Xu et al. for a different symmetry in their filaments than that in Wu et al. collapse completely when one examines the publicly deposited data.
source: In conclusion, the arguments of Xu et al. for a different symmetry in their filaments than that in Wu et al. collapse completely when one actually examines the publicly deposited data.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The micrographs in set04 within the EMPIAR-10014 deposition from Xu et al. (2014) were used for analysis.
source: The micrographs in set04 within the EMPIAR-10014 deposition (http://pdbe.org/empiar) from Xu et al. (2014) were used for analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the data source used in the author's analysis.

claim: Of the 581 images in the dataset, the first 160 were used for filament extraction.
source: Of the 581 images, the first 160 were used for filament extraction.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the author's analysis.

claim: For the 160 images, the mean defocus was 3.2 μ and the range was from 1.7 μ to 5.4 μ.
source: For the 160 images, the mean defocus was 3.2 μ and the range was from 1.7 μ to 5.4 μ.
evidence: This is a statement about the imaging parameters determined from the author's analysis.

claim: From the 160 images, 1066 long filament boxes were cut using the e2helixboxer routine within EMAN2.
source: From these 160 images, 1066 long filament boxes were cut using the e2helixboxer routine within EMAN2 (Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the author's analysis.

claim: Overlapping boxes 192 px long (2.3 Å/px) were cut from the long filament boxes using a shift of 6 px (97% overlap), generating 64,980 boxes.
source: Overlapping boxes 192 px long (2.3 Å/px) were cut from the long filament boxes using a shift of 6 px (97% overlap), generating 64,980 boxes.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the author's analysis.

claim: IHRSR converged to a symmetry of −101.2° rotation with an axial rise of 5.3 Å, starting from a solid cylinder as an initial reference.
source: These were used for IHRSR (Egelman, 2000) which converged to a symmetry of −101.2° rotation with an axial rise of 5.3 Å, starting from a solid cylinder as an initial reference.
evidence: This is a statement about the results of the author's analysis.

claim: The initial reconstruction had a resolution of approximately 17 Å.
source: Due to the very poor resolution (∼17 Å), an attempt was made to improve this by only using the 58 images with a defocus less than 3.0 μ, which yielded 15,624 overlapping boxes.
evidence: This is a statement about the results of the author's initial analysis.

claim: The final reconstruction was generated from 8600 segments after excluding segments with very large out-of-plane tilt.
source: Because segments with a very large out-of-plane tilt were excluded, the final reconstruction was generated from 8600 segments.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods and data used in the author's final analysis.
